question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $(\frac{1}{(x + 4)y}+\frac{1}{y})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1$ that satisfies $y(-3)=e.$

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{1}{(x + 4)y}+\frac{1}{y})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{y}(\frac{1+(x + 4)}{(x + 4)})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{(x + 4)}{(x + 4)+1} \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{(x + 4)}{(x + 4)+1}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (1-\frac{1}{(x + 4)+1})\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =(x + 4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x + 4)+1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{(x + 4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x + 4)+1|+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{(x + 4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x + 4)+1|+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{(x + 4)}\cdot {e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x + 4)+1|}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ y & =\frac{K{e}^{(x + 4)}}{(x + 4)+1},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(-3)=e$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(-3) & =e \\ \frac{K{e}^{1}}{1+1} & =e \\ K & =2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $(\frac{1}{(x + 4)y}+\frac{1}{y})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1$ that satisfies the condition $y(-3)=e$ is

$$
y=\frac{2{e}^{(x + 4)}}{(x + 4)+1}\,.

question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{(x + 4)}^{2}}+{y}^{2}$ that satisfies $y(-5)=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{(x + 4)}^{2}}+{y}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{(x + 4)}^{2}}+1 \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{{(x + 4)}^{2}}+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{{(x + 4)}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =-\frac{1}{(x + 4)}+(x + 4)+C \\ \frac{1}{y} & =\frac{1-{(x + 4)}^{2}-C(x + 4)}{(x + 4)} \\ y & =\frac{(x + 4)}{1-{(x + 4)}^{2}-C(x + 4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{(x + 4)}{1-{(x + 4)}^{2}-C(x + 4)},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(-5)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(-5) & =1 \\ \frac{-1}{1-(-1)^{2}-C(-1)} & =1 \\ \frac{-1}{C} & =1 \\ C & =-1\,.\end{aligned}

$$

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{(x - 4)}^{2}}+{y}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{(x - 4)}^{2}}+1 \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{{(x - 4)}^{2}}+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{{(x - 4)}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =-\frac{1}{(x - 4)}+(x - 4)+C \\ \frac{1}{y} & =\frac{1-{(x - 4)}^{2}-C(x - 4)}{(x - 4)} \\ y & =\frac{(x - 4)}{1-{(x - 4)}^{2}-C(x - 4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{(x - 4)}{1-{(x - 4)}^{2}-C(x - 4)},\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(3) & =1 \\ \frac{-1}{1-(-1)^{2}-C(-1)} & =1 \\ \frac{-1}{C} & =1 \\ C & =-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2(x + 4){y}^{3} & =4(x + 4) \\ 3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(x + 4)(2+{y}^{3}) \\ \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(x + 4) \\ \int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2(x + 4)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}y & ={(x + 4)}^{2}+{C}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the integral on the left-hand side of this equality, we use a substitution

$$
u=2+{y}^{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Then  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{2+{y}^{3}}(3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+{C}_{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})+{C}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where we used that $y>0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})+{C}_{2} & ={(x + 4)}^{2}+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3}) & ={(x + 4)}^{2}+{C}_{1}-{C}_{2} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})} & ={e}^{{(x + 4)}^{2}+{C}_{1}-{C}_{2}} \\ 2+{y}^{3} & =K{e}^{{(x + 4)}^{2}} \\ {y}^{3} & =K{e}^{{(x + 4)}^{2}}-2,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{{C}_{1}-{C}_{2}}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(-4)=1$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}^{3} & =K{e}^{{0}^{2}}-2 \\ 1 & =K-2 \\ K & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
{y}^{3}=3{e}^{{(x + 4)}^{2}}-2.
$$
